verdict:
This is a legal procedural novel set in 1920s Lancashire, following solicitor Prescott as he builds a solemn-form probate case proving a second codicil to a will is a forgery. What distinguishes it from conventional legal drama is its formal conceit: the novel is structured like the file it describes, each chapter closing one door of innocent explanation, the case assembled by documentary accumulation rather than revelation. The climax turns on a single-word discrepancy in a legal recital — "and her issue" where the executed instrument says "or her issue" — a pivot that is prepared from the novel's first chapter and revealed at precisely the right moment. The book's deepest subject is professionalism as moral virtue: Garside's habit of noting what didn't need to be noted, done for its own sake and without foreknowledge of its use, becomes posthumously the mechanism by which the forgery is exposed. "He could not have known it; he had made it anyway." That is a genuine literary subject, and the novel earns it rather than gesturing at it.

The prose is uniformly precise: restricted, period-appropriate without being pastiche, with occasional sentences of real literary quality — the kind that a competent-but-ordinary line would not produce because they require not just skill but a formal understanding of what the novel is doing. The POV design — Prescott as a man whose interiority is expressed entirely through professional action, who never describes his own feelings but only his records — is not a device but a formal necessity. It embodies the book's argument about what professional habit actually means. The countdown structure (days to hearing, entered as marginal notes in working documents rather than as chapter headings) creates procedural tension without announcing itself, and its arithmetic is internally consistent throughout. The characterization of Walter Eccleston — a man who is humanized precisely enough to be comprehensible and damned precisely enough to be guilty — is achieved almost entirely through documents and two brief appearances. His moment of recognition in the corridor of the Royal Courts, reading the executed first codicil for the first time and encountering "or" where he had always known "and," is the novel's most human scene, and it requires no speech.

The weaknesses are real and specific. The chapter header format is inconsistent in a way that reads as an editorial artifact: chapters 1–3 use numeral chapter numbers, chapters 4–6 use written-out numbers, and from chapter 7 onward the chapter number is dropped entirely. No formal logic accounts for the abrupt transition after chapter 6, and the inconsistency within the numbered section (numeral to word after chapter 3) reinforces the impression of an incomplete copyediting pass. The strong-room register entry is quoted identically in full in both chapters 1 and 5; the second reading is partially justified (Prescott re-reads it with new understanding after Garside's death), but the identical block quotation tests patience. More substantially, Garside's death — the structural and emotional hinge of the entire novel — is handled with such professional compression that the loss doesn't land with the weight it requires. Garside has been present as a voice and a handwriting rather than as a person, which is consistent with the novel's method but means the hinge event works more as plot mechanism than as felt experience. Nora Fairhurst, who delivers the novel's sharpest observation in chapter 13, is kept so systematically at POV distance that her character's potential is underused throughout.

This is literature rather than a well-made thing, by a margin sufficient to be interesting. The middle section — roughly chapters 8 through 11, where the profession canvass, the sale contract, and the financial correspondence are laid out — sags relative to the surrounding chapters, the method applied without quite the same elegance. But the novel recovers fully, and the final three chapters are close to exemplary: the corridor, the withdrawal, the return to Winckley Square, the next file opened on a Tuesday in January. The ending is earned from the novel's first page. Readers wanting courtroom drama will be frustrated; readers for whom "the habit was now the proof" reads as a sentence worth a novel will find something genuinely accomplished here.

strongest.claim: The 'or/and' pivot is the novel's formal masterstroke. The discrepancy between 'or her issue' in the executed first codicil and 'and her issue' in the forged recital is established in chapter 16's working note and made explicit in chapter 17 when Prescott reads both instruments side by side. The evidence was present from the novel's first page — the executed codicil text appears in chapter 1 — but neither reader nor protagonist is directed to look for a single conjunction until the structure demands it. The combination with exhibit 14 (Walter's own June 1925 letter, using 'and') closes the authorship question without assertion.

Garside's posthumous presence through his records is the book's deepest literary achievement. The concept that a dead man's professional habit becomes the mechanism of justice — discovered at the hinge in chapter 5, named in chapter 18 ('the habit was now the proof'), and returned to in the novel's final paragraphs — is genuinely earned across the full length of the book. The September 1926 register entry, written more precisely than the occasion required by a man who could not have foreseen why, is the moral centre of the novel.

The corridor scene — Walter reading the executed first codicil for the first time and encountering 'or' where he had always carried 'and' — is the novel's most human moment and its best piece of dramatic economy. Walter's recognition is conveyed entirely through physical gesture ('his head very slightly inclined'; 'He was not large now'), without dialogue or interior access. The withdrawal follows in minutes. The court appearance is brief precisely because the real action has already happened in the corridor.

The POV design is a formal necessity rather than a device. Prescott's interiority, expressed entirely through record-keeping rather than introspection, embodies the novel's argument about professional habit as moral virtue. The design cannot be separated from the book's subject without the book becoming a different and lesser thing. The closing line of chapter 4 — 'The file had always had an address in it — Bank Parade, Preston — but it had been a legal address' — demonstrates how much feeling the method can carry when it is working at full pressure.

The countdown structure (days to the hearing, entered as working-note marginal figures) creates procedural tension without announcing itself as a device. The arithmetic is internally consistent throughout: the 290 days established on 20 December in chapter 5 subtract correctly against every subsequent figure. The countdown is felt as professional pressure rather than authorial contrivance, which is exactly what the novel requires.

weakest.claim: The chapter header format is inconsistent across the manuscript in a way that reads as an editorial production artifact rather than a deliberate formal choice. Chapters 1–3 use numeral chapter numbers ('Chapter 1 —', 'Chapter 2 —', 'Chapter 3 —'); chapters 4–6 use written-out numbers ('Chapter Four —', 'Chapter Five —', 'Chapter Six —'); from chapter 7 onward the chapter number label is dropped entirely and only the title remains. No formal logic accounts for the abrupt transition after chapter 6, and the inconsistency within the numbered section (numeral to written-out after chapter 3) reinforces the impression of an incomplete formatting pass.

The strong-room register entry of 19 September 1926 is quoted in full, as an identical block quotation, in both chapter 1 and chapter 5. The second appearance is partially justified — Prescott re-reads it with new understanding after Garside's death — but the repetition of the same verbatim block, down to the same punctuation and phrasing, over fourteen pages of text, strains patience and risks reading as a production artifact (a section written in isolation, without access to the earlier chapter).

Garside's death is the structural and emotional hinge of the novel — it is the event that makes Prescott sole consciousness, sole custodian, and ultimately the agent of justice — but it does not land with the weight it requires. Garside has appeared as a voice and a handwriting, not as a person with texture, before his death. The relationship of sixteen years is asserted ('He was thirty-eight. He had worked beside this man for sixteen years.') but not built from prior scene or detail. The death works as plot mechanism; it does not work as felt loss.

Nora Fairhurst is the most perceptive character in the novel — her observation in chapter 13 ('He was sorry in the way people are when they have done something they believe they had to do. It was not performed.') is the sharpest single sentence in the book — and she is systematically kept at POV distance by a first-person-adjacent perspective that cannot follow her. The novel's professional male interiority restricts the human texture that Nora could provide, and her appearances in the final chapter are handled with less precision than the legal and documentary material surrounding them.

The middle procedural section sags relative to the chapters before and after it. Chapter 8 (The Gazette) is almost entirely a list of outcomes — forty-six letters sent, forty-six replies received, all negative — stated without the formal elegance that makes the same methodical approach work elsewhere. The chapter establishes a necessary negative result but does not find a way to make the enumeration itself interesting. Chapter 11 (The Sale Contract) is similarly dense with financial correspondence that contextualizes rather than advances, and the nine Walter-to-bank-manager letters, though useful as motive evidence, slow the narrative considerably.

quotes.text: Outside on the square the October light was doing what it did.
quotes.why: The vagueness is pointed and characteristic: Prescott is not a man for atmospheric impressionism. The sentence earns its place precisely by declining to do what another novelist would do with October light.

quotes.text: The file had always had an address in it — Bank Parade, Preston — but it had been a legal address.
quotes.why: The novel's method at its most compressed: an observation about a document that carries the full weight of Prescott's awareness that the Fairhursts are people, not parties. The distinction between legal and human address is the closest he gets to sentiment, and the restraint is the point.

quotes.text: And the file was going to prove a forgery.
quotes.why: The only moment of direct authorial declaration in the novel. Its placement — at the end of the most methodical chapter in the book, after pages of cabinet-searching — gives it the quality of a fact arrived at rather than announced.

quotes.text: A solicitor's clerk crossed the flagstones below, folder in hand, walking with the specific pace of a man carrying something he had not read.
quotes.why: An incidental observation that demonstrates the precision of the novel's attention: the pace of someone carrying something unread is a specific and accurate thing, and noticing it is characteristic of a man who reads documents with the care Prescott applies to everything.

quotes.text: He was sorry in the way people are when they have done something they believe they had to do. It was not performed.
quotes.why: The sharpest single observation in the novel, delivered by Nora Fairhurst about Walter's visit. The second sentence does the work: 'It was not performed' distinguishes between remorse and its performance in two words, and also, indirectly, characterizes the novel's own mode — this is not a performative book.

Walter has been described as 'a man whose presence had always been larger than his physical size.' This four-word reversal, occurring at the moment he reads the executed first codicil and understands what 'or' means, is the climax of the novel. No speech is required.

quotes.text: More precise than the occasion required. He could not have known it; he had made it anyway.
quotes.why: The novel's thesis, stated directly at its close, about Garside's register entry. The two sentences carry the entire argument: habit as virtue, precision as its own justification, the record that outlasts its maker. This is the sentence the book was building toward.

quotes.text: He was not a monster. He went down anyway.
quotes.why: Two sentences that do exactly what the novel has earned the right to do: acknowledge Walter's humanity without forgiving his act. The abruptness — the criminal matter dispatched in six words — is the right proportion.

put_down_points: Chapter 8 (08-the-gazette): The forty-six firm canvass is enumerated rather than dramatized — a methodical list of letters sent and negative replies received. A reader expecting escalating tension in the novel's middle third may abandon here.

Chapter 11 (11-the-sale-contract): Nine Walter-to-bank-manager letters laid out in sequence provide motive context but no discovery. The financial subplot is necessary but this chapter is its thinnest presentation, and readers not invested in the procedural method may not survive the mortgage arithmetic.
who_is_this_for: Readers who find procedural precision aesthetically satisfying rather than merely informative: admirers of Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall for its close-third professional interiority, or of Patrick Hamilton's period realism, or of Sarah Waters' commitment to the texture of a documented world. Lawyers and legal historians who can appreciate both the technical accuracy and the aesthetics of the documentary method. Anyone for whom the phrase 'the habit was now the proof' reads as a sentence worth the novel it took to earn it. Not for readers expecting courtroom speeches, dramatic confession, or conventional detective-novel revelation.
